title: Chronic Pruritus — Initial Workup Pathway
subtitle: Stage-by-stage: history → exam → tier-1 labs → tier-2 labs → imaging → biopsy

items.label: Onset, duration, and rate of progression
items.detail: Define chronicity: >6 weeks = chronic. Was onset sudden (drug) vs gradual (systemic)? Chronic pruritus lasting years before diagnosis is common in Hodgkin lymphoma.

items.label: Distribution: generalized vs localized; palms/soles; anogenital; dermatome
items.detail: Palmar-plantar predominance suggests cholestasis. Dermatomal distribution suggests neuropathic origin. Anogenital-only suggests lichen sclerosus, candidiasis, or contact dermatitis.

items.label: Timing and aggravating factors
items.detail: Nocturnal predominance: scabies, uremic pruritus, cholestatic pruritus. Water-triggered burning within minutes: aquagenic pruritus of polycythemia vera. UV exposure worsens: brachioradial pruritus.

items.label: Personal or family history of atopy, eczema, psoriasis, or allergies
Sick contacts, household contacts — scabies screening
items.detail: Scabies spreads in households and nursing homes. Ask about contacts with similar itch regardless of apparent skin findings.

items.label: Occupational and environmental exposures
items.detail: Wet work (irritant contact dermatitis), fiberglass exposure, chemical agents, latex, fragrances. Occupational context is frequently overlooked.

items.label: Complete medication history including OTCs, supplements, herbal remedies
items.detail: Consider any drug started within 4-12 weeks before itch onset. Key culprits: opioids, ACE inhibitors, statins, chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine, hydroxyurea, chemotherapy agents, checkpoint inhibitors.

items.label: Systemic B symptoms: unintentional weight loss, fever, drenching night sweats
items.detail: B symptoms + generalized pruritus = Hodgkin lymphoma until proven otherwise. Pruritus may precede lymphoma diagnosis by 6 months to 5 years.

items.label: Jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, RUQ pain — cholestasis symptoms
Urinary symptoms, known CKD, dialysis status — renal screen
Neurologic symptoms: burning, stinging, allodynia at specific dermatomal sites
items.detail: Neuropathic itch characteristically has sensory descriptors beyond itch (burning, stinging, formication) and may have no visible rash or only secondary excoriation marks.

items.label: Psychiatric history and psychosocial stressors
items.detail: Chronic pruritus is bidirectionally linked to anxiety and depression. Delusions of parasitosis (delusional infestation) is psychiatric in etiology and requires antipsychotics (pimozide, risperidone) rather than dermatologic treatments.

items.label: Full skin survey including scalp, intertriginous areas, genital, perianal
items.detail: Primary vs secondary lesions must be distinguished. Secondary lesions (excoriations, prurigo nodules, lichenification, lichen simplex chronicus) result from scratching and are not diagnostic of a primary dermatosis. Examine all body surface areas systematically.

items.label: Dermoscopy of suspicious lesions and scalp
items.detail: Linear burrows (scabies), Wickham striae (lichen planus), linear IgA deposits at BMZ may be hinted by morphology. Trichoscopy for scalp itch: perifollicular casts (LPP), Darier sign elicitation for mastocytosis.

items.label: Complete lymph node survey (cervical, axillary, inguinal, epitrochlear)
items.detail: Lymphadenopathy with generalized pruritus mandates lymphoma workup. Bilateral axillary and supraclavicular nodes are particularly concerning.

items.label: Abdominal exam: hepatosplenomegaly, ascites
items.detail: Hepatomegaly suggests hepatic cause. Splenomegaly may indicate hematologic disease (polycythemia vera, lymphoma).

items.label: Thyroid palpation (nodules, goiter, tenderness)
Dermographism test (stroke skin firmly with wooden spatula)
items.detail: Positive dermographism (urticarial line within 3-5 minutes) suggests symptomatic dermographism as a cause or urticarial component to the pruritus.

items.label: Darier sign (stroke pigmented macule/papule to elicit urtication)
items.detail: Positive Darier sign: urtication and erythema within 1-2 minutes of stroking a macule is pathognomonic for cutaneous mastocytosis.

items.label: Neurological assessment at site of localized itch (sensation, dermatome map)
items.detail: Reduced pinprick sensation + burning itch at C5-C8 dermatome: brachioradial pruritus. T2-T6 paraspinal: notalgia paresthetica. Ice pack test: relief with ice application in neuropathic itch.

items.label: CBC with differential
items.detail: Eosinophilia (parasitic infection, drug reaction, mastocytosis, Hodgkin). Leukocytosis + lymphocytosis (lymphoma). Polycythemia (Hgb >16.5 g/dL in M, >16.0 in F): evaluate for PV. Iron-deficiency anemia can cause pruritus without skin findings.

items.label: Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP): LFTs, creatinine, BUN, electrolytes, glucose
items.detail: Elevated ALP + GGT with normal transaminases suggests cholestasis. Elevated creatinine/BUN in context of known CKD → uremic pruritus. Hyperphosphatemia: CKD-associated. Elevated glucose: screen for diabetes-associated neuropathic itch.

items.label: TSH
items.detail: Hypothyroidism causes xerosis and pruritus; hyperthyroidism also causes pruritus via increased sweating and skin vasodilation. Thyroid disease is a common and easily treatable cause.

items.label: Ferritin and iron studies
items.detail: Iron deficiency can cause generalized pruritus without anemia. Ferritin <15 ng/mL is diagnostic. Iron repletion resolves pruritus in documented iron-deficiency cases. Elevated ferritin may indicate hemochromatosis or iron overload in CKD.

items.label: HIV serology (4th-generation Ag/Ab combo)
items.detail: Prurigo of HIV (intensely pruritic papules) is associated with low CD4 count. HIV itself can cause eosinophilic folliculitis and pruritic papular eruption in advanced disease.

items.label: HBV surface antigen + anti-HCV antibody
items.detail: Chronic hepatitis B and C can cause cholestatic pruritus and cryoglobulin-mediated itch. Screen all patients with unexplained chronic pruritus.

items.label: Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) + urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP)
items.detail: Monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance (MGUS), multiple myeloma, or Waldenström macroglobulinemia can present with chronic pruritus. SPEP reveals M-spike; UPEP detects Bence Jones proteins.

items.label: Total IgE
items.detail: Markedly elevated IgE (>1000 IU/mL) may indicate atopic diathesis, parasitic infection, drug hypersensitivity, or hypereosinophilic syndrome.

items.label: Serum tryptase (if mastocytosis suspected)
items.detail: Baseline serum tryptase >20 ng/mL raises concern for systemic mastocytosis and warrants bone marrow biopsy. Normal tryptase does not exclude cutaneous mastocytosis.

items.label: GGT + direct bilirubin (if ALP elevated, to confirm cholestasis)
items.detail: GGT elevation confirms hepatic source of ALP elevation (vs bone). Direct (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia confirms obstructive pattern. Bile acid levels (fasting serum bile acids) are the most sensitive marker for cholestatic pruritus severity.

items.label: Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) for PBC
items.detail: AMA titers >1:40 in the context of elevated ALP and itch are >95% specific for primary biliary cholangitis. AMA M2 subtype is most specific. Confirm with liver biopsy if clinical picture is atypical.

items.label: HbA1c + fasting glucose (if diabetes not yet screened)
items.detail: Diabetes mellitus is associated with generalized pruritus via peripheral small-fiber neuropathy and nephrogenic pruritus in diabetic nephropathy. HbA1c also screens for prediabetes.

items.label: Intact PTH + calcium (if CKD or hyperparathyroid suspected)
items.detail: Secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD contributes to uremic pruritus via calcium-phosphate deposition in cutaneous nerves. PTH-driven mechanisms may be partially independent of dialysis adequacy.

items.label: JAK2 V617F mutation (if aquagenic pruritus or polycythemia suspected)
items.detail: Aquagenic pruritus with elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit warrants JAK2 V617F testing. Present in >95% of polycythemia vera cases. If negative but PV suspected, check JAK2 exon 12 mutations.

items.label: LDH, ESR, uric acid (if lymphoma suspected)
items.detail: Elevated LDH + ESR in context of B symptoms and pruritus: lymphoma work-up required urgently. Uric acid may be elevated in high tumor burden states.

items.label: Abdominal ultrasound (if cholestatic pattern)
items.detail: First-line imaging for suspected biliary obstruction, PBC, hepatic metastases, or splenomegaly. Ultrasound is non-invasive, widely available, and detects bile duct dilation, gallstones, and hepatic parenchymal changes.

items.label: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET-CT (if Hodgkin/NHL suspected)
items.detail: Staging of lymphoma requires cross-sectional imaging. PET-CT is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma staging and response assessment (Deauville criteria). CT alone is acceptable for initial workup if PET is unavailable or contraindicated.
items.branchIf: B symptoms, lymphadenopathy, or elevated LDH present

items.label: MRI cervical spine (if brachioradial pruritus suspected)
items.detail: Cervical radiculopathy at C5-C8 is the most common structural cause of brachioradial pruritus. MRI without contrast: evaluate for disc herniation, neural foraminal stenosis, or cord signal change.
items.branchIf: Localized forearm/dorsal arm itch without rash

items.label: Chest X-ray (mediastinal widening screen for Hodgkin)
items.detail: A widened mediastinum on CXR in the setting of pruritus + B symptoms warrants urgent CT chest. Mediastinal disease is present in >60% of classical Hodgkin lymphoma at diagnosis.
items.branchIf: Rapid screening when CT is delayed

items.label: 4mm punch biopsy from primary lesion edge (if primary lesions present)
items.detail: Obtain from active lesion margin, not the center. Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) for H&E. Request PAS stain for fungal elements if tinea suspicion. Avoid previously treated areas.

items.label: Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) if autoimmune bullous disease suspected
items.detail: Separate 4mm punch biopsy placed in Michel transport medium (saline acceptable short-term) from perilesional non-blistered skin. DIF is the gold standard for BP (linear IgG + C3 at BMZ), pemphigus (intercellular IgG), and lichen sclerosus with autoimmune overlap.
items.branchIf: Urticarial plaques or bullae in older adult, or urticarial-phase BP

items.label: Skin biopsy for small-fiber neuropathy (punch biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fiber density)
items.detail: Reduced IENFD on PGP9.5-stained sections confirms small-fiber neuropathy as a cause of neuropathic pruritus. Performed at distal leg (10cm above lateral malleolus) per standard protocol. Useful in idiopathic generalized itch unresponsive to all treatments.
items.branchIf: Suspected neuropathic or idiopathic pruritus with burning/stinging quality

items.label: Lymph node biopsy (excisional preferred for lymphoma staging)
items.detail: If lymphoma is suspected, excisional lymph node biopsy (not FNA) is required for architectural assessment and accurate subtype classification. Reed-Sternberg cells in Hodgkin, centrocytes in follicular lymphoma. Refer to hematology/oncology for biopsy planning.
